summary: Defines the Structure of Management Information for SNMPv2, the rules and notation used to describe the managed objects that SNMP can read and change. It was replaced by RFC 2578.

plainLanguage.summary: Network devices keep lists of facts about themselves: counters, tables, settings and alerts. This RFC is the grammar for writing those lists down, so that any management program can read them the same way. It fixes the words that may be used, the shape of a name, and the rules for describing a table and its rows.

subtitle: The rulebook for writing down what a network device can report and be told to change.

tldr.problem: Management stations and the devices they manage need a common, precise way to describe the objects, such as counters, tables, settings and alerts, that SNMP reads and changes.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1902 defines a restricted subset of ASN.1 plus three macros, MODULE-IDENTITY, OBJECT-TYPE and NOTIFICATION-TYPE, a small set of base data types, and a naming tree rooted at the Internet subtree 1.3.6.1.
tldr.outcome: Every MIB module written to the same rules can be read by the same management software. The RFC has been obsoleted by RFC 2578, which is the current form of these definitions, and it had itself replaced RFC 1442.

today: RFC 1902 is a Draft Standard published in January 1996 that has been obsoleted by RFC 2578, which is the current form of these definitions. It had itself obsoleted RFC 1442.

sections.title: What the SMI Is For
sections.content:
A management system contains several, potentially many, nodes, each with a processing entity called an agent that has access to management instrumentation; at least one management station; and a management protocol used to convey management information between the agents and the management stations. Operations of the protocol are carried out under an administrative framework that defines authentication, authorization, access control and privacy policies. Management stations run management applications that monitor and control managed elements, which are devices such as hosts, routers and terminal servers.

Management information is viewed as a collection of managed objects residing in a virtual information store, the Management Information Base (MIB). Collections of related objects are defined in MIB modules, and these modules are written using an adapted subset of OSI's Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1). The purpose of the Structure of Management Information (SMI) is to define that adapted subset and to assign a set of associated administrative values.

The SMI is divided into three parts. Module definitions are used when describing information modules, and an ASN.1 macro, MODULE-IDENTITY, concisely conveys the semantics of an information module. Object definitions are used when describing managed objects, and an ASN.1 macro, OBJECT-TYPE, concisely conveys the syntax and semantics of a managed object. Notification definitions are used when describing unsolicited transmissions of management information, and an ASN.1 macro, NOTIFICATION-TYPE, concisely conveys the syntax and semantics of a notification.

For the purpose of exposition, the original Internet-standard Network Management Framework, described in RFCs 1155, 1157 and 1212, is called the SNMP version 1 framework, and the current framework is called the SNMP version 2 framework.
sections.plainLanguage: A device runs an agent, a manager program runs on the other side, and a protocol carries data between them. The data is described in a document called a MIB module. This RFC says what such a module may contain and how each piece must be written, so that a manager written once can read every module.

sections.title: Modules, Descriptors and Names
sections.content:
An information module is an ASN.1 module defining information relating to network management. Typically there are three kinds: MIB modules, which contain definitions of inter-related managed objects and use the OBJECT-TYPE and NOTIFICATION-TYPE macros; compliance statements for MIB modules, which use the MODULE-COMPLIANCE and OBJECT-GROUP macros; and capability statements for agent implementations, which use the AGENT-CAPABILITIES macros. The classification does not imply a rigid taxonomy: a standard information module will normally include definitions of managed objects and a compliance statement, and a standard information module may not contain capability statements.

The constructs of ASN.1 allowed in SNMPv2 information modules include the IMPORTS clause, value definitions for OBJECT IDENTIFIERs, type definitions for SEQUENCEs with restrictions, ASN.1 type assignments of the restricted ASN.1 types, and instances of the ASN.1 macros defined by the SNMPv2 framework. Additional ASN.1 macros may not be defined in SNMPv2 information modules. The names of all standard information modules must be unique, although different versions of the same module keep the same name. An information module may not use the ASN.1 construct of placing an object identifier value between the module name and the DEFINITIONS keyword.

All information modules start with exactly one invocation of the MODULE-IDENTITY macro, which provides contact information and revision history, and it must appear immediately after any IMPORTs statements. Within a module, each macro invocation takes the form of a descriptor, a macro name, clauses and a value. The descriptor corresponds to an ASN.1 identifier: one or more letters or digits whose initial character must be a lower-case letter, and hyphens are not allowed, unlike in ASN.1 itself, so that expressions using a minus sign can refer to these descriptors without ambiguity. Descriptors must be unique and mnemonic and must not exceed 64 characters, though descriptors longer than 32 characters are not recommended. The set of descriptors defined in all standard information modules must be unique. By convention, a descriptor for an object whose syntax is Counter32 or Counter64 should denote plurality.

To reference an external object, the IMPORTS statement identifies both the descriptor and the module in which it is defined. When symbols from enterprise-specific modules are referenced and different objects share a descriptor, the ambiguity is resolved by prefixing the descriptor with the module name and a dot. The ASN.1 EXPORTS statement is not allowed in SNMPv2 information modules: all items defined in a module are automatically exported.

An OBJECT IDENTIFIER value is an ordered list of non-negative numbers. Each number is a sub-identifier, there are at most 128 sub-identifiers in a value, and each sub-identifier has a maximum value of 2^32-1. All values have at least two sub-identifiers, and the first is one of the well-known names ccitt, iso or joint-iso-ccitt.

The root of the subtree administered by IANA for the Internet is internet, that is 1.3.6.1. Several branches underneath it are used for network management: mgmt at 2 for standard objects, experimental at 3 for objects being designed by IETF working groups, and private at 4 for objects defined unilaterally, with enterprises at 1 beneath private used among other things to let providers of networking subsystems register models of their products. The SMI does not prohibit the definition of objects in other portions of the object tree.
sections.plainLanguage: Every fact has a name made of numbers, like a street address that gets more specific at each step. The first numbers are fixed: the Internet sits at 1.3.6.1. Under it, standard objects live under one branch, objects still being designed under another, and a vendor's own objects under a third, where each product can get its own sub-branch. Names are limited in length and in how many numbers they can have, and a name may not contain a hyphen, so that a hyphen in an expression is never confused with part of a name.

sections.title: The Base Types
sections.content:
The SYNTAX clause of an OBJECT-TYPE macro must be present and defines the abstract data structure corresponding to the object. It must be a base type, the BITS construct, or a textual convention; SEQUENCE OF and SEQUENCE are also possible for conceptual tables. The base types are those defined in the ObjectSyntax choice.

Integer32 represents integer-valued information between -2147483648 and 2147483647 inclusive and is indistinguishable from the INTEGER type, though both may be sub-typed to be more constrained. INTEGER may also be used for named-number enumerations, in which case only the enumerated values may appear; although it is recommended that enumerated values start at 1 and be numbered contiguously, any valid Integer32 value is allowed and the values need not be contiguous. OCTET STRING represents arbitrary binary or textual data; there is no SMI-specified size limit, but MIB designers should realize there may be implementation and interoperability limitations for sizes in excess of 255 octets. OBJECT IDENTIFIER represents administratively assigned names, with at most 128 sub-identifiers and each no greater than 4294967295.

The BITS construct represents an enumeration of named bits assigned non-negative contiguous values starting at zero, and only the enumerated bits may be present; there is no SMI-specified limit on the number of enumerations, but there may be limitations for sizes in excess of 128 bits. IpAddress represents a 32-bit internet address as an OCTET STRING of length 4 in network byte order; it is a tagged type for historical reasons. Counter32 represents a non-negative integer that increases monotonically until it reaches 4294967295, when it wraps around and starts again from zero. Counters have no defined initial value, so a single counter value has, in general, no information content; the meaningful quantity is the change between readings. The MAX-ACCESS value for a Counter32 object is either read-only or accessible-for-notify, and no DEFVAL clause is allowed.

Gauge32 represents a non-negative integer that may increase or decrease but never exceeds a maximum, which cannot be greater than 4294967295; the value sits at its maximum whenever the information being modeled is at least that maximum, and decreases if the information later falls below it. TimeTicks represents a non-negative integer giving the time, modulo 2^32, in hundredths of a second between two epochs, which the description of the object identifies; the type may not be sub-typed. Opaque is provided solely for backward compatibility and shall not be used for newly defined object types; it passes arbitrary ASN.1 syntax by encoding it with the Basic Encoding Rules into a string of octets, which is itself encoded as an OCTET STRING. A conforming implementation need only be able to accept and recognize opaquely encoded data. A requirement on standard MIB modules is that no object may have Opaque as its syntax.

Counter64 represents a non-negative integer that increases monotonically until it reaches 18446744073709551615, when it wraps around and starts again from zero, with the same rules about initial values, access and the absence of a DEFVAL as for Counter32. A requirement on standard MIB modules is that Counter64 may be used only if the information being modeled would wrap in less than one hour if Counter32 were used instead. Unsigned32 represents integer-valued information between 0 and 4294967295 inclusive and is indistinguishable from Gauge32.
sections.plainLanguage: Only a short list of value types may be used, and each one carries a promise about its range and its behaviour. A counter goes up until it reaches its ceiling and then starts again from zero, so only the difference between two readings means anything. A gauge goes up and down but stops at its ceiling. Time is counted in hundredths of a second. Anything more complicated has to be broken down into these pieces or left out.

sections.title: Access, Tables and Rows
sections.content:
The MAX-ACCESS clause, which must be present, defines whether it makes protocol sense to read, write or create an instance of the object, or to include its value in a notification. It is the maximal level of access for the object, and this maximal level is independent of any administrative authorization policy. The values are ordered from least to greatest: not-accessible, accessible-for-notify, read-only, read-write and read-create. If any columnar object in a conceptual row has read-create as its maximal level of access, then no other columnar object of the same row may have read-write.

Management operations apply exclusively to scalar objects. It is, however, often convenient to impose an imaginary tabular structure on an ordered collection of objects within a MIB. Each such conceptual table contains zero or more rows, and each row may contain one or more scalar objects, called columnar objects. This is formalized by using the OBJECT-TYPE macro to define both an object corresponding to a table and an object corresponding to a row in that table. A conceptual table has the syntax SEQUENCE OF an entry type, a conceptual row has the syntax of that entry type, and the entry type is a SEQUENCE with one member for each subordinate object. These ASN.1 types are always present, with DEFAULT and OPTIONAL clauses disallowed, and the MAX-ACCESS clause for conceptual tables and rows is not-accessible.

For newly defined conceptual rows that allow the creation of new object instances or the deletion of existing ones, there should be one columnar object with a RowStatus syntax and read-create access, which by convention is the status column of the row.

The INDEX clause, which must be present if the object corresponds to a conceptual row unless an AUGMENTS clause is present instead and must be absent otherwise, defines instance identification information for the columnar objects subordinate to that object. It must specify objects whose values unambiguously distinguish a row, and the syntax of those objects indicates how to form the instance identifier: an integer-valued object gives a single sub-identifier; a fixed-length string gives one sub-identifier per octet; a variable-length string gives the length followed by one sub-identifier per octet; an object identifier-valued object gives one sub-identifier per sub-identifier of the value; and an IpAddress-valued object gives four sub-identifiers in the familiar a.b.c.d notation. The IMPLIED keyword can only be present for a variable-length syntax and only on the last object in the clause. Instances identified by integer-valued objects should be numbered starting from one.

Objects that are both in the INDEX clause of a row and columnar objects of that same row are called auxiliary objects, and their MAX-ACCESS is not-accessible, except in a module originally written for SNMPv1 and later converted, or where a row must contain at least one columnar object that is not an auxiliary object, in which case one of them must be at least read-only.

The AUGMENTS clause is the alternative to INDEX and names the object corresponding to the base conceptual row that this row augments; a row augmentation cannot itself be augmented, and a base row may be augmented by several augmentations. When defining instance identification information for a conceptual table, the AUGMENTS clause should be used if there is a one-to-one correspondence between the rows of this table and an existing table; otherwise, if the relationship is sparse, an INDEX clause identical to that in the existing table should be used; and otherwise, if no existing objects have the required syntax and semantics, auxiliary objects should be defined within the conceptual row and used in the INDEX clause.

The STATUS clause, which must be present, indicates whether the definition is current or historic: current and obsolete are self-explanatory, while deprecated means the definition is obsolete but an implementor may wish to support it to foster interoperability with older implementations. The DESCRIPTION clause must be present and contains a textual definition providing all the semantic definitions necessary for implementation. The DEFVAL clause, which need not be present, defines an acceptable default value that an agent may use when an object instance is created; the value must correspond to the object's syntax. Object types with a syntax of Counter32 or Counter64 may not have a DEFVAL, since they have no defined initial values, though it is recommended that they be initialized to zero.
sections.plainLanguage: Each object says how much access it makes sense to have: read only, read and write, or read, write and create. Objects are grouped into tables, and a table is a set of rows with the same columns. The INDEX clause says which values identify a row, and AUGMENTS is the alternative for a table that adds columns to an existing one. The status column is the one a manager writes to in order to create, change or delete a row.

sections.title: Revising a Module
sections.content:
As experience is gained with a published information module, it may be desirable to revise it. To begin, the invocation of the MODULE-IDENTITY macro should be updated to include information about the revision, usually by updating the LAST-UPDATED clause and adding a pair of REVISION and DESCRIPTION clauses, though other existing clauses may also be updated. The module's label, such as the FIZBIN-MIB of the example in the document, is not changed when the module is revised.

If any non-editorial change is made to any clause of an object assignment, then the OBJECT IDENTIFIER value associated with that object assignment must also be changed, along with its associated descriptor. An object definition may be revised in a limited set of ways: a SYNTAX clause containing an enumerated INTEGER may have new enumerations added or existing labels changed; a STATUS clause value of current may be revised as deprecated or obsolete, and deprecated as obsolete; a DEFVAL clause may be added or updated; a REFERENCE clause may be added or updated; a UNITS clause may be added; a conceptual row may be augmented by adding new columnar objects at the end of the row; and entirely new objects may be defined with previously unassigned OBJECT IDENTIFIER values. If the semantics of any previously defined object are changed, that is, if a non-editorial change is made to any clause other than those specifically allowed, then the OBJECT IDENTIFIER value must also be changed. Changing the descriptor associated with an existing object counts as a semantic change, since these strings may be used in an IMPORTS statement. If the STATUS clause value of an object changes, the DESCRIPTION clause should be updated accordingly.

A notification definition may be revised by adding or updating a REFERENCE clause; otherwise a change in the semantics of a previously defined notification requires a new OBJECT IDENTIFIER value, and changing the descriptor counts as a semantic change.
sections.plainLanguage: A module can be revised, but the rule is that you may not quietly change what an existing name means. Adding a new value to a list, marking something as deprecated, adding a default or a reference, or adding a column at the end of a row are all allowed. Anything that would change the meaning of a name that managers already use requires a new name, so that old managers keep working with the old meaning.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section of this memo is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo.

The reason is visible elsewhere in the document. The SMI defines notation and naming only, so the protection of a management exchange comes from the administrative framework of the SNMP framework, which defines authentication, authorization, access control and privacy policies. One point deserves emphasis because it is easy to misread: the MAX-ACCESS clause states the maximal level of access that makes protocol sense for an object, and it is explicitly independent of any administrative authorization policy. In other words, read-write in a MIB module says that writing the value is a meaningful operation; it does not say that anyone may perform it.
sections.plainLanguage: This note is only the rulebook for labels, so it says nothing about locks. The locks are handled elsewhere, in the framework that decides who may read and who may write. A label that says an object can be written does not promise that the reader will be allowed to write it.

viz.caption: THE BASE TYPES AND WHAT EACH ONE PROMISES

items.label: -2147483648 to 2147483647
items.desc: Whole numbers, the same as INTEGER, and may be narrowed further.

items.label: 0 to 4294967295
items.desc: Whole numbers that never go negative; indistinguishable from Gauge32.

items.label: 0 to 4294967295
items.desc: Increases until it reaches the maximum, then wraps to zero. A single reading means nothing; the change does.

items.label: 0 to 18446744073709551615
items.desc: The same as Counter32 but 64 bits wide; only for values that would wrap in under an hour.

items.label: 0 to 4294967295
items.desc: May go up or down but never exceeds its maximum; it stays at the maximum while the value being modelled is at least that high.

items.label: Hundredths of a second
items.desc: A time measured modulo 2^32 between two epochs the object description names.

items.label: 4 bytes
items.desc: A 32-bit internet address as an OCTET STRING in network byte order.

items.label: Arbitrary bytes
items.desc: Binary or text data, with no size limit in the SMI.

items.label: Named bits
items.desc: An enumeration of bits numbered from zero, where only the named bits may be present.

items.label: Backward compatibility only
items.desc: Carries arbitrary ASN.1 syntax encoded twice over; not to be used in new object types.

items.label: not-accessible
items.desc: An auxiliary object, such as a table, a row or an index.

items.label: accessible-for-notify
items.desc: Reachable only through a notification, such as the trap identifier.

items.label: read-write
items.desc: May be read and written, but not created.

items.label: read-create
items.desc: May be read, written and created.
